Let us start where everybody starts. Walk me through what you do now, and tell me why you are drawn to this role.
I draft and review commercial contracts in-house, and last year I took ownership of our contract templates. I am drawn to this role because you are opening the office my clients keep asking me about.
The job involves negotiating in English most weeks. Everybody tells me they enjoy that. Tell me about a time it went badly.
A supplier agreed to a cap and then asked to remove it the night before signature. I remember reading the new draft at eleven and deciding to stop the whole thing.
So you stopped a signature to protect one clause. Did anybody thank you that week?
Nobody. Three months later the same supplier missed a deadline, and my boss remembered to mention it in front of the board.
Good answer. Here is the one nobody prepares for. What is your blind spot — what would your team say about you that you would not say about yourself?
I would rather answer that honestly than well. I tend to assume that people read what I send them. I have learned to say the important thing twice: once in writing, once out loud.
Let me walk you through what I actually did.
The role involves negotiating in English, which is exactly what I am drawn to.
I tend to assume that people read what I send them, so I have learned to say it twice.
That is a good question, and I would rather think for five seconds than answer badly.

The question people call the curveball is not there to catch anybody out. I have never asked one because I wanted to watch somebody suffer. I ask it because by minute twenty I have heard the prepared answers, and the prepared answers all sound the same, and I still do not know how this person thinks when there is nothing ready to say. That is the whole job. Nobody has ever paid a lawyer for the answer they had prepared in advance. The candidates who worry me are the ones who have rehearsed everything, because they are excellent for twenty minutes and then the first real question arrives and there is nobody home. So here is my advice, and it costs nothing. When the hard question comes, say out loud that it is a good question and take the time. In fifteen years of hiring I have never once turned somebody down for thinking for five seconds.

When I put two candidates in front of a partner and their experience is identical on paper, the interview decides it, and it usually decides it on one thing. Most answers about strengths come out as adjectives. I am organised, I am proactive, I am detail-oriented. Adjectives are free. Anybody can claim them and nobody can check them, so they carry no weight at all. What I want is a story with a date in it, a decision and a consequence: this is what happened, this is what I did about it, and this is what came of it afterwards. Three sentences is often enough. And to the people working in their second language, who apologise to me before they even start: you do not lose points for your grammar. You lose them for hiding behind an answer that is three words long. A long story told imperfectly beats a short one told beautifully, every single time.

A shortlist is drawn up, and somebody decides that you are worth an hour of their day. The hiring manager opens by asking you to walk her through what you do now and why you are drawn to the role. You answer with examples rather than adjectives, and she stops you in the middle to ask when it happened and what came of it. Then a curveball arrives, the question nobody could have prepared for, and you take five seconds before you say anything at all. At the end you ask your own questions, which is where they find out whether you would be a good fit.
